parole.significato: A simple plough consisting of a spike dragged through the soil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Norwegian ard (“plough”), from Old Norse arðr, from Proto-Germanic *arþrą (“plough”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom (“plough”), whence also Latin aratrum.

parole.significato: Tautogolabrus adspersus, a wrasse native to the western Atlantic, inhabiting inshore waters near the sea floor at depth…
parole.testo: From Norwegian berggalt (“a labrid fish”), equivalent to berg (“mountain, hill; rock”) + galte (“boar”).

parole.significato: A large rucksack.
parole.testo: Shortened from Bergen rucksack, possibly named after their creator, Norwegian Ole F. Bergan, combined with the name of the Norwegian city of Bergen.

parole.significato: A sprat (small herring), especially Sprattus sprattus.
parole.testo: From Norwegian brisling and Danish brisling, from Low German bretling, from bret (“broad”), from Middle Low German *brêd, from Old Saxon brēd.

parole.significato: Synonym of brunost
parole.testo: A calque from Norwegian brunost (“brown cheese”).

parole.significato: A brown Norwegian whey cheese with a strong, sweet flavor.
parole.testo: From Norwegian brunost (literally “brown cheese”), from brun + ost.

parole.significato: An ancient Norwegian musical instrument, made from the horn of a ram or goat, traditionally used by cowherds.
parole.testo: From Norwegian, from bukk (“buck”) + horn.

parole.significato: A quirky, silly or stupid, socially inept person, or one who is out of touch with contemporary trends and typically has…
parole.testo: First use appears in the US c. 1961. The sense of a "silly person" is presumably from earlier use as a bowdlerization of dick (“penis”) in student slang, particularly the Midwest. Despite a common misconception, it has never referred specifically to a whale's penis, but penises in general. Alternati

parole.significato: Unpaid voluntary, orchestrated community work.
parole.testo: From Norwegian dugnad, from Old Norse dugnaðr (“help”).

parole.significato: The great northern loon, Gavia immer.
parole.testo: Calque of Norwegian emmer-gaas.

parole.significato: A Norwegian salted, dried, and cured leg of lamb
parole.testo: From Norwegian fenalår.

parole.significato: A thermal boot made from reindeer skin and fur.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Norwegian finnesko, from finn (“Sami”) + sko (“shoe”).

parole.significato: A long, narrow, deep inlet between cliffs.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Norwegian fjord, from Old Norse fjǫrðr, from Proto-Germanic *ferþu, *ferþuz (“inlet, fjord”), from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”), from *per- (“to carry forth”) + *-tus (suffix forming action nouns from verb roots). Doublet of firth, ford, port, and fjard.

parole.significato: brunost
parole.testo: Borrowed from Norwegian geitost (“goat cheese”), which is geit (“goat”) + ost (“cheese”), from Old Norse geit + ostr.

parole.significato: Synonym of Hardanger fiddle.
parole.testo: From Norwegian hardingfele.

parole.significato: In Norwegian history, an informal retinue of personal armed companions, hirdmen or housecarls.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Norwegian hird, from Old Norse hirð, a borrowing from Old English hīred, hēored (“family, household”), from Proto-West Germanic *hīwarād (“relationship; family”), equivalent to hewe + rede. Cognate with German Heirat (“wedding”).

parole.significato: A member of a Norwegian hird, or royal household.
parole.testo: Calque of Norwegian hirdmann; equivalent to hird + -man.

parole.significato: A type of supernatural being in the shape of a beautiful woman with a cow's tail.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Norwegian hulder, with the same meaning.

parole.significato: A Swedish and Norwegian cocktail (from the Trøndelag region) containing coffee together with moonshine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Norwegian karsk, from Old Norse karskr.

parole.significato: Synonym of kransekage.
parole.testo: From Norwegian kransekake.

parole.significato: Any of several small marine crustacean species of plankton in the order Euphausiacea in the class Malacostraca.
parole.testo: From Norwegian krill (“fry of fish”).

parole.significato: A Norwegian cookie invented by emigrants to America, prepared as a rolled-up cone, sometimes with a filling.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Norwegian krumkake (“curved cake”). Compare Middle English crumcake, cramkake (“loaf of unleavened bread; a twisted or crumpled cake”).

parole.significato: A Norwegian stew of diced meat and vegetables, similar to scouse.
parole.testo: From Norwegian lapskaus, which was borrowed again from English lobscouse.

parole.significato: A traditional soft Norwegian flatbread made from potato, flour, and milk or cream (or sometimes lard) and cooked on a g…
parole.testo: From Norwegian lefse.

parole.significato: A wingless bipedal dragon; a lindworm.
parole.testo: From Norwegian linnorm.

parole.significato: A long-distance (approximately 35+ kilometer) cross country skiing event.
parole.testo: From Norwegian løpet.

parole.significato: a spitz dog originating in Norway, traditionally used for hunting puffin.
parole.testo: From Norwegian lundehund, compound of lunde (“puffin”) and hund (“dog”).

parole.significato: A traditional Nordic dish made from stockfish and soda lye.
parole.testo: From Norwegian lutefisk, compare with Swedish lutfisk.

parole.significato: A minor complaint or problem.
parole.testo: First attested in 1599. Origin uncertain, but likely borrowed from dialectal Norwegian nigla (“to be stingy, to busy oneself with trifles”), ultimately from Old Norse hnøggr (“stingy; miserly”), related to Old English hnēaw (“stingy; niggardly”). More at niggard.

parole.significato: A breed of dog of the spitz type, used as an all-purpose farm and herding dog, as well as a watchdog and a nanny dog.
parole.testo: From Norwegian + Norwegian buhund, from bu (“homestead, a simple building or mountain hut (where the shepherd lived while looking after his herd in the summer) but can also mean stock, as in livestock”) + hund (“dog”).

parole.significato: A low-slung boatlike sled, used for man-hauling supplies across snow and ice.
parole.testo: From Nordic languages: Norwegian pulk; Swedish pulka, Finnish pulkka, from Sami pul’hkē (compare Northern Sami bulki), from Proto-Samic *pulkkē.

parole.significato: A Norwegian delicacy consisting of raw trout fermented after being packed moist with salt.
parole.testo: From Norwegian rakfisk.

parole.significato: A sei whale.
parole.testo: From sei whale, from Norwegian seihval, seikval, from sei (“pollock”) + hval (“whale”). Doublet of saithe.

parole.significato: A whale of the rorqual family (Balaenoptera borealis).
parole.testo: Partial translation of Norwegian seihval, seikval, from sei (“pollock”) + hval/kval (“whale”).

parole.significato: An alternative or variant form of a word or morpheme.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Apparent etymologies include a learned borrowing from Norwegian sideform, a calque of German Nebenform, and a compound of side + form.

parole.significato: Any young herring (other than a sprat), especially if canned and processed in Scandinavia for sale as a sardine.
parole.testo: From Norwegian and Danish sild, from Old Norse síld. More at sile. See also sillock.

parole.significato: A Norwegian fishing boat classification, for boats around 10 metres in length, between 25 and 40 feet, and with a parti…
parole.testo: From Norwegian sjark, from Russian, from English shark.

parole.significato: A type of tobogganing in which competitors lie face down, and descend head first.
parole.testo: The etymology of the term is disputed between two versions. * From the sled used, which originally was a bare frame, like a skeleton. * From Norwegian kjaelke (a type of ice sled) through a bad anglicization as "skele".

parole.significato: One of a pair of long flat runners designed for gliding over snow or water.
parole.testo: From Norwegian ski, from Old Norse skíð (“stick of wood, snowshoe”), from Proto-Germanic *skīdą (“stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, split”) (see also shed). Cognate with Old English sċīd (“stick of wood”) (modern shide), Old High German skit (Modern German Scheit (“log”)).

parole.significato: To cross-country ski behind one or more dogs or horses, or a vehicle.
parole.testo: From Norwegian skikjøring, from ski + kjøring (“driving”) (see kjøre (“to drive”)).

parole.significato: The winter sport of a person being towed on skis, especially by sled dogs
parole.testo: From Norwegian skikjøring.

parole.significato: To race in a slalom.
parole.testo: From Norwegian sla (“steep, hill side”) and låm (“trail”).

parole.significato: A Norwegian style of folk music or dance, or a piece of such.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Norwegian slått.

parole.significato: To stray, rove, or wander from a normal course and others of its kind.
parole.testo: From Middle English straglen, of uncertain origin, possibly from (or cognate to) dialectal Norwegian stragla (“to walk laboriously”).

parole.significato: A coastal landform consisting of a near-flat erosion surface typical of the Norwegian coast.
parole.testo: From Norwegian strandflate, a compound of strand (“beach”) and flate (“surface; plain; level area”). The E is not present because of comparison to flat (relatively level surface of land).

parole.significato: A unit of measure of volume transport, used in oceanography, equal to 1 million cubic metres per second.
parole.testo: From Norwegian Sverdrup. After Harald Sverdrup (1888–1957), Norwegian oceanographer and meteorologist.

parole.significato: Telemark skiing, a method of skiing using the telemark turn and a binding that only connects the boot to the ski at the…
parole.testo: From Norwegian Telemark, a county in Norway, from Old Norse Þelamǫrk, from the genitive plural case of þelir (“name of an old Germanic tribe”) + mǫrk (“borderland, march, mark, woodland”).

parole.significato: A fit of pettishness, or slight anger; a tiff.
parole.testo: Compare Norwegian teft (“a scent”). See tiff (“noun”).

parole.significato: Expressing surprise, dismay, relief, exhaustion, or a sudden shock to the senses.
parole.testo: From Norwegian, brought to the US by Scandinavian settlers.

parole.significato: The unpleasant after-effects of the consumption of alcohol; a hangover.
parole.testo: From Norwegian kveis (“uneasiness after debauchery”) + -algia (pain, suffering) (from New Latin -algia, from Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”)), coined as a medical term by Jeffrey G. Wiese, Michael G. Shlipak, and Warren S. Browner in a 2000 article published in the Annals of Internal Medicine (s

parole.significato: Yacht.
parole.testo: From Norwegian jaght, from Middle Low German jacht, short for jachtschip (“fast pirate vessel”). More at yacht.

parole.significato: A type of two-man keelboat from Norway.
parole.testo: From Norwegian yngling, Danish yngling, Swedish yngling (“youngster”); from Old Norse ungr (“young”) + -lingr (diminutive suffix, compare -ling), also a surname in Old Norse. Doublet of youngling.
